analysis.title: Higher Yields Keep Traders Paying Up For Protection
key_insights: Treasuries are getting some relief on Tuesday, but elevated rate vol and rich payer skew show the market is wary of another move higher in yields.

Bear steepening remains the dominant theme despite Tuesday's pause. Softer payrolls and more patient Fed rhetoric have pushed the probability of an October hike below 25%, so the front end is outperforming.
The long end has not benefited from a less-urgent Fed. A less-urgent Fed does not imply a lower terminal rate or ease concerns over fiscal deficits and heavy Treasury supply.
ISM Services Prices Paid jumped to 74, the highest since July 2022. Uncertainty around energy costs and AI-related capex demand reinforce the possibility that yields keep grinding higher.
The MOVE Index is near its highest this year. One-month implied volatility on TLT is around the 98th-100th percentile over the same period, in contrast with subdued equity volatility.
Citi research finds long-expiry payer skew and Treasury put skew rich, meaning investors are paying an unusually high premium for protection against a further rise in yields.
The backdrop can be self-reinforcing. Rising yields tend to lift long-dated volatility and extend mortgage duration, prompting additional hedging that can add selling pressure.
The market is technically oversold, but the catalyst for a durable reversal is unclear. Deutsche Bank shows CTAs heavily short bonds, while JPMorgan's Treasury clients are net long.

This week's 10- and 30-year auctions matter more than normal. A clean absorption of supply offers a route to stabilization, while another weak reception would validate what options already imply: yields have yet to hit cycle highs.
